correctness.rationale: After clearing positive denominators, the identity is equivalent to \(2^r p^s(2^{k+1}-1)=(2^k-1)(2^{r+1}-1)\sum_{i=0}^s p^i\). The \(k=1\) case is ruled out by strict lower bounds. For \(k\geq2\), the coprimalities force \(2^k-1\mid p^s\). Elementary modulo-eight and odd-factor arguments show that \(2^k-1\) is never a proper power, so \(p=2^k-1\). The reduced equation yields \(p^{s-1}\mid 2^{r+1}-1\) and \(2p+1=t[p^{s-1}+2\sum_{i=0}^{s-2}p^i]\) for positive integer \(t\). At \(s=2\), this requires \(1<t<2\), and for \(s\geq3\) it requires \(t<1\); hence \(s=1\). The remaining equality forces \(r=k\), and direct substitution verifies sufficiency. Independent finite integer computation tests 256,512 profiles and 576 direct divisor-enumeration profiles, supporting rather than replacing the proof.

originality.rationale: The complete primary 2015 paper treats harmonious-pair sparsity and discordance, not the exponent-uniform prime-support exclusion. The closest publicly indexed exact theorem explicitly restricts the odd prime to exponent one, namely partners \(2^r p\); that \(s=1\) case is acknowledged as covered. The new part eliminates every repeated odd-prime factor \(p^s\) for \(s\geq2\) and arbitrary positive exponents \(k,r\), which is not implied by an iff statement on \(s=1\). Bishop et al. (2021) consider the equation under the feebly amicable alias without giving the repeated-prime obstruction. Actual alias, exact, database, and stronger-coverage searches identified no theorem settling the added cases, while incomplete coverage and full-text-access limits remain residual risks.
residual_risks: The indexed published prior exact theorem was retrievable as title and mathematical abstract, not its complete proof; an auxiliary stronger statement inside its inaccessible manuscript cannot be ruled out absolutely.
Other earlier nonindexed equivalent classifications of reciprocal abundancy ratios might exist; negative search results do not certify universal novelty.

value.rationale: Harmonious-partner recognition at the smallest nontrivial prime-support complexity is a natural structural problem originating in published work. The sharp theorem extends beyond the already covered squarefree-odd-part case by excluding every repeated odd-prime exponent uniformly, not merely moving a finite bound. It requires denominator rigidity, exclusion of Mersenne proper powers, and an exact integer factor squeeze. It distinguishes a complete rigid two-prime-support family from unrestricted partners with more prime factors and requires no hypothetical infinitude of Mersenne primes.
